Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-11 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Leah Morris (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood Solutions), Nina Park (Head of ML - Orbit), Marcus Liu (Platform Eng - Orbit), Priya Sharma (SRE - Orbit), Evan Kline (Data Eng - Orbit)

---
Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- 72h run showed average KV hit 42% but heavy long-tail misses during bursts
- Prefetch reduced tail latency but increased token cost by ~18% in the test window
- Prompt variants decreased key overlap; simple normalization improved prefix reuse ~12%

---
00:00 Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, quick sanity check on video and audio?
00:12 Nina: we can hear you, all good on this end.
00:18 Samir: Cool. So agenda — quick metrics, hypothesis on TTL vs prefetch tradeoffs, then tuning items and next steps. Leah will walk the numbers.
00:30 Leah: Hi, hey all — I pulled the last 72 hours from the pilot cluster, and uh, main takeaways: overall kv/prefix combined hit rate averaged 42%, but median response latency when cache hit was 85ms and miss cases showed heavy tail up to 1.2s during restart windows.
01:05 Marcus: That 1.2s — is that before or after our edge router? We're seeing some additional overhead in our sidecar.
01:12 Leah: Good call, Marcus, our traces include edge time; cold path breakdown we sent had about 140–180ms from edge, so runtime miss accounted for roughly 900–1,000ms in the worst cases.
01:28 Nina: The reason we tried long TTLs originally is to avoid those warm spikes. But cost spiked when prefetch was on in the alpha test — can you quantify the token delta?
01:39 Leah: Yes — the controlled prefretch (soft prefetch for top 20% sessions) increased token consumption by ~18% across the window; prefetch recaptured about half the miss latency but at that cost.
02:05 Diego: Quick terminology: I'm going to call hard prefetch the synchronous fetch on session start and soft prefetch the background speculative fill — we saw the latter less disruptive but cost-additive.
02:20 Evan: On our side, the prompt fuzz is large — many short prompts differ only by entity IDs which makes cache keys unique; that explains low overlap.
02:33 Leah: Right — we ran a prompt normalization where we replaced ids with placeholders and coalesced similar templates; that increased prefix reuse by ~12% in a synthetic replay.
02:50 Priya: How realistic was the replay? Did it preserve arrival patterns and backpressure?
03:00 Leah: It did preserve arrival times from the 72h logs but we truncated some long-running sessions for safety; so it's not perfect, but directional.
03:15 Nina: I want to focus on TTL levers — if we shorten TTLs we'll reduce stale cache and maybe reduce token churn, but then warm restart spikes could get worse. Thoughts?
03:30 Samir: Yes, it's a tradeoff. Short TTL reduces opportunity cost of prefetching the wrong context, but increases frequency of refills. Two knobs we recommend testing together: a shorter TTL baseline (2–10 minutes) plus targeted soft-prefetch for heavy users, and prompt coalescing before cache keying to boost overlap.
04:00 Marcus: Do we have numbers for hit-rate lift vs TTL?
04:07 Leah: From the 72h replay: TTL 30m baseline -> combined hit 42%. TTL 10m (no prefetch) -> hit fell to 35% but avg cost per real request fell slightly because fewer stale tokens were emitted. With TTL 10m + soft-prefetch top10% -> hit back up to 48% and tail latency improved.
04:38 Evan: Interesting — so prefetch recovers hit-rate but at token cost; and coalescing could amplify that benefit.
04:46 Diego: Another axis is eviction policy — LRU tends to favor recent sessions but LFU or weighted might favor long-running active users. For our workload we have many one-off queries which hurts LRU.
05:06 Leah: We prototyped a weighted eviction that biases keys with higher reuse count and it improved hit-rate for the top 20% cohorts by about 8% in the replay.
05:20 Priya: But complexity increases for us if we have to maintain counts across sharded caches. Are we talking local counts or global?
05:29 Leah: The Redwood runtime supports local per-shard LFU-ish counters with periodic sync; it's approximate but cheaper than global counters.
05:40 Marcus: About the cost math — can you show the end-to-end per-100k requests delta?
05:46 Leah: Sure, rough numbers from the test: baseline TTL30m (no prefetch) = $X per 100k requests (we had an anonymized cost model in the doc). TTL10m + soft-prefetch(top10%) = +18% token cost -> net $X*1.18 per 100k, but user-perceived latency improved by median 220ms.
06:12 Nina: We care more about P95 latency and session continuity. Median is useful but P95 and P99 spikes during restarts are what break UX.
06:22 Leah: Right — we saw P95 drop from 800ms to 420ms with the soft-prefetch hybrid.
06:30 Samir: There's also opportunity in smarter normalization: coalescing entity IDs and removing non-informative boilerplate reduces unique keys. That can be cheap and give lift without token cost.
06:45 Evan: We tried a lighter normalization in prod and saw a 6% reuse improvement immediately but worried about over-normalization affecting answer quality.
07:00 Leah: We have a testing harness where we can score quality degradation (ROUGE-ish and a small eval set). In the synthetic run, quality delta was within noise for the light normalization. We will, of course, avoid normalizing user-provided instructions or semantics.
07:20 Marcus: On warm restarts we saw a correlated traffic spike when our autoscaler brought pods up — is that because clients retried or because sessions reconnected?
07:30 Priya: Our logs show a mix — some clients retry aggressively, some reconnect and trigger cold flows. We should probably add jittered backoffs on the client and incremental warmup to reduce simultaneous misses.
07:45 Samir: Redwood can implement a staged warmup where only a fraction of the routing goes to warm instances while others are allowed to hit a cheaper fallback until KV warms. That reduces simultaneous misses but can complicate routing rules.
08:00 Nina: Cost vs complexity again — we prefer minimal changes on our side. Could Redwood provide a managed warmup curve?
08:08 Leah: Yes, we can provide a warmup policy that integrates with your autoscaler signals; we'll include an example in the runbook.
08:18 Diego: Actionable experiments to run: 48h controlled run (A) TTL10m + soft-prefetch top10% + coalescing, (B) TTL2m + no prefetch + weighted eviction, (C) TTL30m baseline. Compare hit-rate, P95, token cost, and quality.
08:40 Samir: Perfect. We'll prepare the harness and a notebook to replay.
08:45 Marcus: For logs we need to sanitize keys — we'll strip IDs but keep template shapes so you can replay accurately.
08:52 Evan: We'll share the S3 link to sanitized logs once Marcus confirms.
08:56 Leah: Also want to flag an anomaly from yesterday: a series of long prompts with embedded tables caused our prefix engine to generate multiple keys per user session which depressed hit-rate. We include a suggested trimming rule in the doc.
09:12 Nina: Ok, trimming sounds fine; prefer to keep minimal transformation.
09:18 Samir: Quick question — any regulatory or residency constraints we should recall for storing cache keys?
09:24 Nina: Cache keys are allowed but anything that can be mapped to PII needs to be hashed and kept in EU-only region for some customers. We'll add that to the constraints doc.
09:36 Leah: Noted — we'll include an encrypted, region-aware cache option in the config diff.
09:43 Priya: One operational note: when switching TTLs we should monitor eviction churn rate and set an alert threshold — too high churn means wasted CPU.
09:52 Leah: Agreed — we'll include eviction churn metrics in the dashboard and a recommended SLO for churn percent.
10:00 Samir: All right, quick recap and owners, then we'll wrap.
10:06 Samir: Owners — Samir to send config diffs and cost projection; Leah uploads runbook and harness; Orbit to share sanitized logs and run the 48h experiments; follow-up review scheduled for 2027-08-18.
10:26 Nina: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
10:30 Meeting ends.
